packet.evaluation_question: Explain uncertainty when maternal history, culture results and a later clinical assessment are unavailable.

evidence.text: If there are any risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection (see box 1 on risk- factors for early-onset neonatal infection), or if there are clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (see box 2 on clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection): • perform an immediate clinical assessment • review the maternal and neonatal history • carry out a physical examination of the baby, including an assessment of vital signs. [2021]
Interpret cerebrospinal fluid results in babies alongside the clinical presentation and maternal history. [2024]

The Kaiser Permanente neonatal sepsis calculator can be used as an alternative to the framework outlined in recommendation 1.10.3 for babies born after 34+0 weeks of pregnancy who are being cared for in a neonatal unit, transitional care or postnatal ward. It should only be used if it is part of a prospective audit, which should record: • total number of babies assessed using the calculator • number of babies correctly identified by the calculator who develop a culture-confirmed neonatal infection • number of babies incorrectly identified by the calculator who do not develop a culture-confirmed neonatal infection • number of babies missed by the calculator who develop a culture-confirmed neonatal infection. [2021]

Offer antibiotics during labour to women, trans men and non-binary people who: • are in pre-term labour or • have group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection during the current pregnancy or • have had group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection in a previous pregnancy, and have not had a negative test for group B streptococcus by enrichment culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on a rectovaginal swab samples collected between 35 and 37 weeks' gestation or 3 to 5 weeks before the anticipated delivery date in the current pregnancy or • have had a previous baby with an invasive group B streptococcal infection or • have a clinical diagnosis of chorioamnionitis. [2021]

claims.text: When maternal history, culture results, and later clinical assessment are unavailable, the presence of any known risk factors or clinical indicators creates uncertainty that mandates treating the infant as potentially infected.

support.quote: If there are any risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection (see box 1 on risk- factors for early-onset neonatal infection), or if there are clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (see box 2 on clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection):

claims.text: Perform an immediate clinical assessment of the newborn, including vital signs and physical examination, to gather objective data that can partially compensate for missing maternal and microbiology information.

support.quote: carry out a physical examination of the baby, including an assessment of vital signs.

claims.text: Serial monitoring of inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP) and vital signs should be instituted, recognizing that early trends may be limited without baseline maternal data.

support.quote: review the maternal and neonatal history

claims.text: Escalate to full sepsis work‑up (including blood cultures and lumbar puncture) if clinical indicators worsen or if any new risk factor emerges, because the initial uncertainty cannot be resolved without culture results.

support.quote: Interpret cerebrospinal fluid results in babies alongside the clinical presentation and maternal history.

claims.text: Explain to parents that, due to incomplete maternal and laboratory information, the care team must act cautiously and may initiate antibiotics while awaiting further data.

support.quote: review the maternal and neonatal history

claims.text: Document the uncertainty explicitly in the medical record and consider prospective audit of decisions made under incomplete information, as recommended for tools like the sepsis calculator.

reasons: C1: Evidence only mandates immediate assessment, not treatment; claim overstates guidance.
C3: Evidence does not address serial monitoring of CRP or vital signs; claim lacks support.
C4: Evidence relates to CSF interpretation, not escalation criteria; claim not supported.
C5: Evidence does not cover parent communication or antibiotic initiation; claim unsupported.
C6: Evidence supports prospective audit for sepsis calculator use, not general documentation of uncertainty; claim exceeds evidence.
C1: Evidence only instructs to perform assessment when risk factors/indicators are present; it does not state that uncertainty mandates treating the infant as potentially infected.
C3: Cited evidence refers to reviewing maternal/neonatal history, not to serial monitoring of inflammatory markers or vital signs.
C4: Evidence discusses interpretation of CSF results alongside clinical presentation and maternal history, not escalation to full sepsis work‑up based on worsening indicators.
C5: Evidence about reviewing history does not address parent communication or the need to explain uncertainty and possible antibiotic initiation.
C6: Evidence describes prospective audit requirements for the sepsis calculator, not a general recommendation to document uncertainty or audit decisions made under incomplete information.
